title: Chapter 116 – Seven Fires
html:
[Azure Cloud Sect – Lin Jian]

Eleven months later.

The formula takes four hours to come out of the bench, and it is not a recipe. It is a wall.

Jian stands in the round room of the second tier at the end of the long autumn with the Reservoir lamp low and his arms folded across his chest, and watches the writing climb the curved gray stone. It rises from the floor in slow bright lines of Interface script, row upon row, fine as the veins of a leaf. The register has been running for a month. He has asked it one question, in six different ways, and each time it has said that it needed more time.

Now, at last, it has answered.

```
OPERATOR ARK-7 :: QUERY 31
SUBJECT: THE NEXT STEP (PURPLE MANSION, QI TRACK 9)
STATUS: FEASIBLE. NOT SAFE. NOT CHEAP.
REQUIRED: SEVEN FIRES, TEMPERED IN ORDER.
PURPLE MANSION PILL (BENCH-ASSISTED), 7 REAGENTS:
I. SILVERTHREAD, MOON-VEINED, 7 YEARS. (LIVING.)
II. EMBER CORAL, RED RIDGE VAULT. (STORED.)
III. STARFURNACE ASH, NINE-FURNACE RESIDUE. (STORED.)
IV. MOON DEW, DRAWN FROM A LAN LEAF. (RARE.)
V. SOUTHERN FIREORCHID, FOUR-SEASON. (TRADED.)
VI. OPERATOR'S OWN BLOOD, THREE TIMES TEMPERED. (YOURS.)
VII. THE FIRE OF THE GATE. HELD BY: THE KEEPING.
COST: 90 CE. SEAL STRAIN: SEVERE. TIME: 49 DAYS.
WARNING: ANY OMISSION COLLAPSES THE PILL. THE SEVENTH FIRE CANNOT BE SYNTHESIZED.
```

He reads it from the top, then from the bottom, then from the top again.

Seven, he thinks. Six that can be found. One that cannot be made.

He knows the first three at a glance. Silver-thread grows in his mother's Garden, but only the oldest beds, the ones sown the year he came back from the mountain; a plant of seven winters, silvered through with moon-veins that glow faintly in the dark. Ember coral is a thing Heng left in a vault in Red Ridge. Starfurnace ash is Bai's: the soot of the Nine Furnace Room, gathered grain by grain for forty years in a jar on the old man's highest shelf.

The fourth, the fifth and the sixth he can only guess. Lan Tong would have the moon dew. The Tan southern road would have the orchid. And the blood is his, the red thing in his veins. It must be drawn, and cooled, and warmed, and cooled, and warmed again, and each of the three times it costs him a measure of the soul.

But the seventh.

The Fire of the Gate. Held by the Keeping.

He had hoped it would be a metal, or a stone, or a bottle he could pay for. It is none of those. The register is quite plain. It is a flame, one single flame, that has been kept burning on the ridge for six hundred years in a lantern, and has not once been allowed to go out.

He knows the lantern. He saw it lit in the dusk, on the night he took his provisional seat at the Pill Hall.

Ridge-house. Cloud Peak.

The Quiet Seat.

* * *

The family hears it in the Garden Hall, over a table spread with plain food and nobody eating.

He tells them all of it. It is a habit he has acquired over the years, one he does not wholly understand. There is Wenyuan at the head of the table, with his spectacles pushed up on his forehead. There is Qinghe beside him with a cup of tea going cold. Feng, in his Foundation Middle gray, stands against the wall with his arms crossed. Hu sits with a bowl of rice and a face like a closed fist. Yao and Yue are on the bench by the brazier. And at the far end, small and upright in her gray Elder's robe, her stick across her knees, sits Ye, who has come in the dusk through the east gate, because Jian asked her.

When he has finished there is a silence that goes on for some time.

"Seven winters," says Wenyuan at last.

"What?"

"The silver-thread. Seven winters, moon-veined. That is the east bed, the oldest. We have six hundred plants in it." He rubs his nose. "I would need to ask your mother which are the finest."

"The fourth row," says Qinghe quietly. "The ones by the wall. They were the first you transplanted."

"We would lose the harvest of the east bed," says Yao.

"We would lose more than that." Wenyuan sets down his chopsticks. "The east bed carries the Sect tribute. Four hundred stones' worth of herb, due at the winter assessment. If we pull the finest plant for a pill, we pull the quota with it."

"Then we pay in stones."

"We do not have four hundred stones."

"Then we pay in other things," says Qinghe.

Everyone looks at her.

She meets their eyes, a small plain woman in a brown shawl with silver in her hair, and her voice does not change. "Hu has the forge. I have the stall. Yue has the school. We give up a season. A single season, of tribute and of profit and of new stock. It will mean a thin winter for everyone." She looks at her husband. "It will not mean we starve."

"Mother," says Jian.

"Do not say it." She lifts her hand. "I know what you were going to say. That you do not want the clan to pay. That it is your road, not ours." Her mouth moves. "You do not understand what a family is, Jian. It is the people who carry your road with you, whether you ask them to or not."

Nobody speaks. Then Hu, who has not said a word the whole evening, pushes back his bowl.

"I'll melt the spare quiet blades," he says gruffly. "Sell the metal. Cost a season's work and some pride. But it'll fetch a hundred and twenty."

"Hu—"

"Don't." The big man looks at his plate. "Boy, I spent seven years drunk. Let me spend a season sober on something that matters."

Wenyuan laughs, once, a dry cracked sound, and pushes his spectacles down onto his nose. "Then the clan has a plan," he says. "Heaven help us all."

"The Sutra Hall will pay the rest," says Ye from the end of the table. They all turn. She has not moved, and her face is as blank as ever, but there is a faint color in her papery cheeks. "The Sutra Hall owes your family a debt. I will take it out of the library's tithe. It will be a scandal. I look forward to it."

* * *

He pays the Tan debt next, and it is not cheap either.

Tan Ruyan receives him in the long counting room of her uncle's house in the lower town, behind a desk covered with ledgers, with a brazier at her feet and a brass abacus under her hand. She is twenty-six now, hard and lean and ink-stained, with her black hair in a plain knot and a jade ring on her finger that marks her the house's acting head. Her great-uncle Huai died last winter in his sleep. Her uncle Boren was found, a month later, to have been paying the Registry for twenty-two years. He now keeps accounts in a back room in the south, under guard.

"Southern fire-orchid," she says. "Four-season. I have two."

"I need one."

"I have two, and I need both. They are for a marriage contract." Her pen taps the desk. "But I do not suppose you would have asked if you could do without."

"No."

"Then there is a price." She looks up. Her dark eyes are quite steady. "The Tan seal on the Garden's goods has been worth, by my count, eleven hundred stones in two years. You have not asked for a share. I have not offered one. That ends tonight."

"Say it."

"I want the Garden's name on the southern road. In writing, on a contract. The Lin Garden Hall, Associate House of Tan. I want it carried on our caravans and our ledgers, so that the Cloud Peak Hall cannot strangle us one at a time." Her mouth thins. "It will make you a target. They will say you are a merchant clan with a Sect seat. They will say worse."

"They say it already."

"Then you have nothing to lose." She holds out the contract, a single sheet, already written. "Sign."

He signs. The brush is steady. The ink dries on the plum-white paper like a small black wound, and Ruyan folds it in three and tucks it into her sleeve.

"It will bring you trouble," she says.

"It will bring me an orchid."

"That too." She almost smiles. "And Jian."

"Yes?"

"The paper I offered you, at the Pill Hall. The one that gave you my place. I have burned it." She looks at the flame. "I wanted you to know. It was not a sacrifice. It was an investment. I am the kind of woman who keeps her accounts."

* * *

Bai gives him the ash without a word, and then spoils it by speaking.

The old Elder takes him into the Nine Furnace Room at midnight, shuts the door, and climbs a stool to the highest shelf. He comes down with a jar of black glazed clay no larger than a man's two fists, stoppered with wax. He sets it on the table between them. It is dull and cold and entirely without ornament.

"Forty years," he says. "Every grain from every firing. I've never used it. I told myself I was saving it for something worth the name."

"Elder, I cannot—"

"You cannot what? Take a jar of soot?" Bai sniffs. "It's yours, boy. I decided the day you brought me the crucible. I don't owe you for it. I just don't want it to rot on the shelf." He pushes the jar across. "It will do what you need. Starfurnace ash is the first of the fires, they say. The one that teaches the rest to burn."

"The first?"

"The first of the seven. The old books count them up from the furnace." His eyes narrow. "You've worked out what the seventh is."

"Yes."

"Hm." He chews. "I thought you might. There's a story in the Pill Hall that the Fire of the Gate was once an ordinary flame. That it was kept alive by a man who did not want to be forgotten. That it has been fed ever since with the breath of the sleeping." He shrugs. "I don't know. I'm a pill-maker. I know only that a fire fed for six hundred years on something other than oil is not a fire I'd want to put in a man's belly."

"I have no choice."

"There's always a choice." The old man's voice is gruff. "It's only that they're all bad."

* * *

Yao brings the ember coral up from Red Ridge in the dark of the following week.

He goes alone, with Bei, on foot, along the old east road. It is a three-day walk each way, and he returns on the fourth night with the mud of two counties to his knees and a long flat box wrapped in oilcloth under his arm. He lays it on the study table and unwraps it with unsteady fingers, and does not speak until the lid is open.

Inside, nested in straw, is a branch.

It is as long as a forearm, branching like a hand, and it is the color of an ember seen through smoke: a deep orange-red with a core of white. It gives off a faint, steady heat that Jian feels on his face from three feet away. A sealed letter lies beside it. The seal is Heng's.

"It was in the vault," says Yao, hoarsely. "Behind the old door. The one with the Zhao mark. My uncle said in his letter that it was the last thing our house had of value, and that it should be given to the one who gave us back our name." He swallows. "I do not know what it is. I only know I have been afraid to look at it for nine months."

"It is ember coral."

"It is ours."

"It is yours," Jian says gently. "I only need to borrow it."

"Then borrow it." Yao closes the lid. His hands are shaking. "My uncle was a stubborn man. I do not think he would mind being useful."

In the corner of the room, Hui, fourteen and thin, sits on a stool with his chin on his knees, watching the box. He has not spoken. But when his brother turns away, the boy puts out one hand, very slowly, and lays two fingers on the lid, and the wood under them glows, faintly and for a moment, a clear deep red.

* * *

The moon dew arrives by leaf.

He finds it one dawn on the Pill Hall's bottom step, a seven-lobed Lan leaf the length of his hand, curled into a small green cup, and in the cup, perfectly round and perfectly still, a single bead of clear liquid that glows faintly silver in the gray light. There is no note. There is no footprint in the frost. The bead trembles when he lifts it and does not spill.

He knows the hand. He has known it since the Forty Steps.

Bring the third fragment to the Dock, Lan Tong had said. Not to the House.

The leaf is a reminder, and a payment, and a question. He tucks it into his belt as carefully as he would an egg.

* * *

It is Shen Yuxian who asks the real price.

The invitation has been waiting six years. He receives it at last on a bright cold morning in the second month, a card of thick white paper with a seal of pale blue wax, brought to the Pill Hall by a silent girl in the sky-colored robes of the Cloud Peak Hall. It says only: The Hall regrets the delay. Tea, at your convenience. He takes Ye, as Qin Hao advised. He takes Feng, as a witness. They climb the long white steps in silence, past the pine gate and the pool and the high sunlit terraces, until they reach the house of the Cloud Peak Hall: a long low building of pale stone and blue tile, with a roof like a wing, and a garden that looks as though it has never once been walked in.

Yuxian meets them on the terrace.

She is thirty-three, slender and cool and entirely still, in a robe the color of the sky just before rain. Her hair is bound with a single silver pin. Her face is long and fine and calm as an unlit lamp. She has been a Core disciple for eleven years, and she has been in seclusion for four, and she looks as though she has stepped, this morning, out of a painting of herself.

"Gate Bearer," she says. "Elder Ye. Lin Feng. Forgive the waiting."

"We are glad to be asked," says Ye, in a voice that implies otherwise.

"No one is glad to be asked to this house." Yuxian smiles very faintly. "But I would not have asked unless I had to. Will you walk with me?"

She leads them through the garden, along a path of white gravel, between rows of pruned pines. At the end of the path there is a small, plain pavilion with its screens drawn. She slides one aside.

Inside, on a low bed of pale jade, lies an old man.

He is perhaps eighty. He is thin to the bone, with a long white beard combed over his chest, and his hands are folded on a blue silk coverlet. His eyes are closed. His chest rises and falls so slowly that Jian has to count to see it. At the foot of the bed a small brass lamp is burning, with a flame the color of milk.

"My master," says Yuxian. "Shen Wuping. Elder of the Cloud Peak Hall. He has been asleep for five years."

"I am sorry," says Jian.

"You are not. You have not met him." Her calm is perfect. "But he is the one who kept my brother and me from the House's attention for most of our childhood. He told us what the plum-bark was. He told us, when I was twelve, never to sign anything on it. And one night five years ago he went into his study to burn a letter, and he did not come out."

"A sleep."

"A keeping." She turns her head. "That is what the physicians call it, when they will say anything. I have had every healer in the Sect. I have had a Core Elder sit by him a month. He is not ill. He is not dying. He is held."

Ye steps forward and looks at the old man for a long time. She does not touch him.

"The Quiet Seat," she says softly. "That is what they did to the Head."

"I think so."

"And you want us to look."

"I want the Gate Bearer to look." Yuxian's eyes rest on Jian. "He is the only person in the Sect who can see what I cannot. I have watched him. For six years. I have seen his hands move, in the Hall of Weights, in the Court. I have seen the way he looks at a wall before he looks at a man." She says it without accusation. "I do not need to know how. I only need to know what is there."

He thinks of the cost: two points. He has forty-one. He thinks of the lamp burning, and the flame in it the color of milk.

He lets his eyes go soft, and opens the Door in Autumn.

* * *

The old man in the bed is a lattice of thread.

They run from his crown, from his throat, from his wrists and the soles of his feet. They are fine as spider silk and silver-gray and very, very taut. They rise through the roof of the pavilion in a bundle as thick as a man's arm and run north across the mountain, in a single bright line, toward the ridge.

And at the foot of the bed, beside the brass lamp, there is a second line.

It is not silver-gray. It is a warm clear gold. It runs from the flame of the lamp to a small bronze box beneath the bed, and from the box into the floor, and from the floor, down, into the dark of the mountain.

He follows it with his eyes as far as he can. It goes down, and down, and out of sight.

The Keeping, he thinks. Not a place. A network.

"Gate Bearer?" says Yuxian quietly.

"He is held." He closes the Door. His mouth is dry. "By the same hand that holds the Sect Head. The threads run to the ridge. I can see them. I do not know how to cut them."

"But it can be done."

"I think it can be done by one who holds the fire."

He had not meant to say it. It comes out as a breath, an instinct. Yuxian's eyes sharpen.

"The Fire," she says. "Then you know what hangs on the ridge."

"I know that it is a lantern."

"It is a lantern that was lit by the First Keeper, and tended by thirty-one successors, and carried up the stair on the night of the last Offering." Her voice is perfectly even. "It is not guarded by men. It is guarded by the House. It is the one thing in the Sect they will not lend, or sell, or let out of their sight." She stands very still. "But it can be taken, on the right night, by one who is invited."

"Invited."

"By the Head of the Cloud Peak Hall." She says it quite gently. "Which, in my master's absence, is me."

The wind turns over the pavilion. The lamp at the foot of the bed flickers, and steadies.

"I will give you the lantern," says Yuxian. "I will open the ridge-house on the night of the first snow, and lead you to the room where it burns, and look the other way. In exchange, you will do for my master what you will do for yours."

"I have not got a master."

"You will have a chance to wake my teacher, and the Head of the Sect, and every other sleeper in that house." She does not blink. "But only if you do it in the same breath, with the same hand, on the same night. Because the threads are one thread. And if you cut one, you cut all."

"They will know."

"They will know. The House will feel every cord go slack at the same moment, from the Keeper to the least of its Numbers." Her voice does not shake. "And so I am asking you to choose. Take the lantern, and burn the Keeping. Or leave it, and keep the Fire, and let him sleep."

She looks at the old man on the jade bed, and her face for an instant is not calm at all.

"I have waited five years," she says. "I will wait until the first snow. After that, I will not be able to ask again."

* * *

He walks down the mountain in the late afternoon with Ye's stick tapping on the stones at his side and Feng behind, and for a long time none of them speaks.

The sky is clear and cold and very bright. The pines are black against it. Down in the valley, small as toys, the roofs of the Garden show among the winter fields, and beyond them the long gray shoulder of the Gate stair, and the town, and the road.

"Well?" says Ye at last.

"She is telling the truth."

"She is telling the truth she knows."

"The Head is held. Her master is held. There is a flame at the foot of the bed, and a thread of gold running into the mountain. If I take the Fire, it will cost the Keeping its light." He stops. "And I will have woken forty sleepers at once, and not one of them will know where they are."

"Or you leave the Fire where it burns."

"And I cannot finish the pill."

"No."

"Six reagents. Without the seventh, nothing." He looks down at his hand. "Purple Mansion is the gate to everything beyond. If I do not pass it before the Offering, I will stand in front of the Keeper as I am now. A Foundation. Alone."

"That is not alone," says Feng, from behind.

"You know what I mean."

"I do." His brother comes level with him, and for a moment they walk side by side, the stooped old woman between them. "And I know you will do what you must. I only want you to know that you will not be asked to do it twice."

"What do you mean?"

"If you take the lantern, and they come, they come for us all." Feng's voice is quiet and level. "The clan. The Zhao. Ruyan. Bai. We have counted. We are two hundred and eighty-four. We would rather fight. That is all."

"It is not a thing I can ask."

"No. It is a thing we have already decided."

Jian lifts his eyes to the far ridge.

Against the clear cold sky, tiny and bright as a spark, a single golden point is burning at the top of the mountain, and has burned, he knows, for six hundred years.

The first snow, he thinks. Nineteen days.

Take the Fire, and burn the Keeping. Or keep the sleepers, and lose the road.

And there is no third door.
